meta.title_plain: How two creators made science feel like a superpower
meta.teaser: A writer and an artist turned glass, radios and water wheels into Dr. Stone.

page.title: How two creators made science feel like a superpower
page.sub: The story of Riichiro Inagaki, Boichi and Dr. Stone
page.bigIdea: In Dr. Stone, the hero doesn't win with punches. He wins with science, and the creators made it work through patient research and teamwork.

cards.title: A hero who keeps counting
cards.front: In Dr. Stone, the whole world turns to stone. Senku stays awake inside the stone and counts.
cards.back: He counts every second for 3,700 years. Writer Riichiro Inagaki wanted a hero who wins by working step by step, not a superhero.
cards.tryit: Count to 60 in your head, then check a clock. How close were you?

cards.title: A writer who asked for help
cards.front: Before Dr. Stone, Inagaki wrote Eyeshield 21, an American football manga, from 2002 to 2009.
cards.back: He could have drawn it himself. But he felt like a rookie, so he teamed up with artist Yusuke Murata. It sold over 20 million copies in Japan.
cards.tryit: Think of a skill a friend is better at. Plan one project you could make together.

cards.title: An artist who studied physics
cards.front: Boichi was born in Seoul, South Korea, in 1973. He wanted to draw manga from childhood.
cards.back: So he studied physics in college, to get ready to draw science fiction. Inagaki was a big fan of his art and brought him onto Dr. Stone.
cards.tryit: Draw one machine from your world, like a game controller, with every small detail.

cards.title: Homework behind every invention
cards.front: Senku builds glass, radios and even phones from scratch. How did the creators get the science right?
cards.back: They had a science helper named Kurare. They did real research, like visiting a glass-blowing factory. Boichi kept a library of 900,000 photos to draw from.
cards.tryit: Take 10 photos of interesting things at home or the tennis club. Start your own drawing library.

cards.title: The page that changed everything
cards.front: In one chapter, Senku's team builds a water wheel to make electricity. Inagaki wanted it to look cool.
cards.back: Boichi drew a giant full-page picture of the power plant. Fans loved it. After that, big inventions got big pages, and the team learned each other's strengths.
cards.tryit: Draw your proudest moment, like a winning shot, as one big full-page picture.

quiz.q: Why did Inagaki team up with an artist for Eyeshield 21?
opts: He felt like a rookie at drawing
His editor banned him from drawing
quiz.hint: Think about how confident he felt about his own drawing.
quiz.why: He felt too new to draw it himself, so he found a great artist to partner with.

quiz.q: What did Boichi study in college to get ready for science fiction manga?
quiz.hint: It's the science of forces, motion and energy.
quiz.why: He studied physics so his science fiction drawings would make sense.

quiz.q: Inagaki asked Kurare why radio waves happen. What did Kurare say?
opts: He didn't fully understand it either
It was too easy to explain
quiz.hint: Even experts reach the edge of what they know.
quiz.why: Kurare said he didn't understand it either, which shows science still has mysteries.

quiz.q: What did the water wheel page teach the team?
opts: Let big inventions shine in big pictures
quiz.hint: Fans loved that page. What would you do more of?
quiz.why: Fans loved the giant picture, so big inventions got big pages from then on.

page.think: Senku counted every second for 3,700 years. What's one small thing you could do every day, in tennis or LEGO, that would add up to something big in a year?
